Hello, Adrian Lim. This is Rachel Tan calling for our scheduled portfolio review. Is this still a convenient time to speak? I have allowed time for the conversation, so there is no need to fit everything into a hurried exchange. If you are still in the office, we can leave room for any interruptions rather than trying to talk over them.

Hello, Rachel. Convenient, yes. I'm in the small meeting room, not at my usual desk. At my desk, people see me sitting there and immediately got something to ask. Here at least they have to knock. I've put my papers beside me and told the office I'm on a personal call. No need to rush today. Usually I say that, then somebody brings in a delivery problem, but this time I've actually handed the phone to my colleague.

That sounds like a more comfortable arrangement. Before we begin the review, we can complete the identification formalities.

My FIN is T five three eight three seven six four A. My date of birth is the fifth of January nineteen sixty-seven.

Thank you. How has the transition at the family business been going? When we arranged this call, you were trying to make more room in your working day. I do not want to assume that simply being away from your desk means you have managed to step back from everything.

Stepping back is the difficult part, lah. The team can manage the routine work, actually. It's me who keeps looking over their shoulders. I walk past the dispatch area, see a stack of papers, then ask what happened. After that, of course they bring the next stack to me. Cannot blame them. Now I'm trying to stay out of the daily dispatch discussion unless there's something genuinely unusual. My cousin handles that side, and he knows the customers well. I still like to hear what's happening, just not be the person answering every small question.

There is a distinction between staying involved and being the default person for every decision. From a practical perspective, does your day now have a quieter stretch when people know you are not available for routine matters? That would also help us arrange future banking conversations without repeatedly catching you between office interruptions.

After the delivery arrangements have settled, usually better. Before that, everyone moving around, drivers calling, warehouse asking where to put something. Even if the problem has nothing to do with me, I can hear it through the wall. Later, the office becomes calmer. The trouble is I use that quiet period to catch up on everything else. Then my wife calls and asks whether I'm coming home, and I say I'm just finishing. That phrase, she doesn't believe anymore. Just finishing can mean I've not even opened the last folder yet.

Then it would help if an appointment with us had a clear place in the day, rather than being something squeezed into whatever time remains. We can discuss your preferred calling routine before we finish. For today, are you comfortable staying in that room, or would you prefer to move somewhere with less office noise?

This room is fine. Air conditioning a bit enthusiastic, but I brought my jacket. The noise doesn't bother me so much if nobody expects an answer. Actually, hearing the business outside is quite comforting. Been around that sound for so long. What I don't want is to sit in here and still have messages arriving asking whether I've seen the messages. My colleague knows where I am. If something genuinely needs me, he'll knock. Otherwise, they can work it out.

Good. I will speak at a measured pace, and if someone does knock, simply let me know. You mentioned your cousin taking more responsibility. Has that changed the sort of work you enjoy doing when you are in the office, or are you still finding yourself drawn back to the familiar daily tasks?

Still drawn back, especially when an old customer calls. They ask for me because they know my voice. Sometimes they don't even have a problem; they just want to talk about how business used to be. I enjoy that part. What I enjoy less is being copied on every discussion about cartons and missing signatures. My cousin has started bringing me a short overview instead of the whole pile. At first I kept asking where the rest was. He told me, very politely, that the whole point was not to give me the rest. Fair enough, hor.

It sounds as though he is comfortable explaining the arrangement to you, which is useful in a family business. I imagine those conversations can be different when the people involved are also relatives. Do you still have time together outside work, or does the business tend to follow everyone into family gatherings?

It follows us right to the dining table if we let it. My mother will ask whether everyone has eaten, and before the food is passed around somebody is talking about a customer. Then the younger ones disappear because they know what's coming. Recently we've been better. My wife will ask about somebody's holiday or somebody's garden, quite deliberately. She's not subtle, but it works. I don't want every family meal to feel like an extension of the office. We can care about the business without making everybody listen to it all evening.

That is an understandable distinction. Family time can become difficult to protect when everyone shares the same working background. You also mentioned wanting to spend more time outdoors. Have you been able to get back to the garden, or has that been waiting for the quieter office routine to become established?

The garden doesn't wait for me, unfortunately. Leave it alone and it becomes very confident. I went out after being busy at work and found the creeper had decided the neighbouring pots belonged to it. My wife said that plant has the same management style as me: supposed to stay in its own area, but keeps interfering. I couldn't argue. Mostly I enjoy clearing things and seeing what has come back after the rain. Not trying to produce a show garden. If it looks alive and I can sit outside without stepping over equipment, I'm happy.

That sounds more like a place you can enjoy than another project with a deadline. What do you tend to grow? I ask because people sometimes describe gardening as relaxing, then explain an elaborate routine that sounds as demanding as their working day.

Mostly leafy plants, some flowering shrubs, and herbs near the kitchen. The herbs are more my wife's department. She remembers which leaves belong in which dish. I just make sure I don't pull out something useful by mistake. I used to keep labels, but the weather faded them, and then I thought I could remember. Very confident at the time, completely useless later. Now I ask before moving anything. The nicest part is being outside early, before the road gets busy. No conversation needed. Just look around, do a bit of watering, then have breakfast.

It is good to hear there is something in your week that does not require constant conversation. Do you usually garden alone, or has it become a shared family activity? I will not keep you on the subject if you would rather move on, but it sounds as though you have been enjoying it.

Alone most of the time. My wife joins me when there's something she wants moved, then suddenly it's a shared activity. The children help if they're visiting and I don't make it sound like work. Ask them to come outside for a drink, they're there. Ask whether they can help with the pots, suddenly got another appointment. I'm exaggerating a bit. They do help. I also don't want them spending their visit doing chores just because I left everything until they arrived. Better to have a proper meal together and hear what they've been doing.

That fits with what you said about not letting the business take over family gatherings. It sounds as though you are trying to enjoy being together without always giving the occasion a task. Has that also influenced the sort of travel you prefer now?

Definitely. We went away recently and deliberately chose somewhere quiet near the coast. No big programme. In the past I would arrive with a list, then get irritated if the weather changed or a place was closed. This time my wife said we could simply walk, eat, and see what we felt like doing. At first I kept asking what came next. After a while, stopped asking. We found a small place for breakfast where nobody was trying to move us along. I think I enjoyed that more than the famous attractions we used to queue for.

Was it easy to disconnect from the office while you were away? A quieter destination can still feel busy if the telephone keeps bringing the working day with it. I am interested in how you found the experience, rather than assuming that being away automatically made it restful.

The beginning wasn't restful because I kept checking. Nothing urgent, just habit. I'd take out the phone while waiting for coffee and then find myself reading a long office discussion. My wife could tell immediately from my face. After that I left it in the room when we went for a walk. The office had the hotel details if something serious happened, but nothing happened. That was the slightly embarrassing part. I came back and everything had carried on. Good news, of course, but also a reminder that I'm not holding the roof up personally.

That must have made the quieter days feel different once you stopped following the office discussions. What did you enjoy most about the place itself? Some clients prefer being near a town even on a quiet holiday, while others want to be away from shops and traffic altogether.

Near a town, but not right in the middle. I like being able to walk somewhere for food without turning every meal into an expedition. We had a path near the water and a garden behind the place where we stayed. Nothing grand. There was an old bench that looked as if it had been repaired many times, and I kept sitting there. My wife took a photograph because she said we'd travelled all that way for me to inspect somebody else's plants. But that's what I like now. Ordinary places where you can linger and nobody asks whether you've finished.

There is a clear difference between wanting quiet and wanting to be completely isolated. It sounds as though you found a comfortable balance. Did you bring any of that feeling home, or did the usual working routine take over as soon as you returned?

Some of it came home. I unpacked properly instead of leaving the bag beside the cupboard while I went straight to the office. Small thing, but my wife noticed. We also started walking after dinner when the weather allows. Not exercise with a target, just walking around the neighbourhood. Sometimes we talk about family things; sometimes we complain about the pavement. Very ordinary. The difficult part is not deciding to do it. It's remembering, when work gets noisy, that I actually prefer my day when there's room for that kind of thing.

I appreciate you describing it. It helps me be more considerate about when and how we contact you. For future appointments, would you prefer us to work around the office routine you described, or would a call when you are away from the office be less distracting?

Office is still better for a proper conversation. At home, I don't want banking papers spread across the dining table. Then somebody clears the table and puts them somewhere sensible, which means I cannot find them. Here I've got my folder, a proper chair, and a door. The important thing is arranging it rather than calling when I'm walking through the warehouse. If I know there's a call, I can settle myself. If the phone catches me while I'm halfway through something, I sound available but my attention is somewhere else.

That is useful to know. We can use an arranged office call as your general preference and check your availability when scheduling. Would you rather receive a brief scheduling message first, instead of having an unexpected telephone conversation about finding a suitable time?

A brief message first would be easier. Just say you're trying to arrange a conversation and let me reply when I'm at my desk. No need for a long message. Sometimes I see a big block of text while I'm between things and think I'll read it properly later. Then later becomes much later. Also, please don't assume that because I've opened something I've dealt with it. My family makes that mistake too. They say, you saw the message already. Seeing and doing are very different, lah.

I will distinguish between a scheduling reply and simply having sent you a message. If you are travelling or taking personal time, you can tell us when arranging an appointment. There is no need to discuss that with the office team. Do you prefer to coordinate these calls yourself rather than through a member of your staff?

Myself, please. The office team can keep the room free, but they don't need to manage my personal appointments. They've got enough work already. And I don't want someone trying to be helpful by guessing when I'm free. My calendar can look empty when I'm actually driving somewhere or sitting with my mother. If I reply myself, at least you know I've looked at the day properly. Today worked well because I put the papers here before the office became busy, instead of searching for them while you waited.

That arrangement is clear. We have covered quite a lot of the practical background without needing to rush into the paperwork. Before we turn to the review itself, is there anything about the telephone setup or the way you have your notes arranged that would make it easier to follow the conversation?

The setup is fine. I use the handset for this, not the speaker. On speaker I end up looking around the room and losing the thread. I've got a clean page beside my own notes. I like keeping what I say separate from what somebody summarises back to me. Otherwise I look at it afterwards and cannot remember whether a phrase was mine or whether I just wrote it down because I heard it. Not saying anybody is doing anything wrong. It's just how I keep myself from getting muddled.

You can keep your notes in that format, and I will leave space when you need to write. There is no need to answer while you are still finding a page. I recommend selling Meridian Asia Equity Fund.

Hmm. Let me sit with that for a moment. I've got the relevant papers here, but I don't want to move from chatting straight into talking faster than I'm thinking. This is where I usually put the pen down first, then read what I've brought. Otherwise my hand is busy and my ears are only half working. The office can wait; I made room for this call.

Take the time you need. I will listen while you set out what you want to discuss, and we can keep the conversation orderly. You do not need to fit your remarks into the way your papers happen to be arranged.

For this transaction, the holding I want you to deal in is Meridian Asia Equity Fund. I want to sell from my existing holding. For the transaction and settlement currency, I'm considering Japanese yen. Let me finish working through the details first. I've left some space on my page because I don't want everything running together. If I stop speaking, it's probably because I'm looking at my notes, not because the line has dropped.

Your objective, then, is to reduce your exposure to Asian equities and free up funds for anticipated personal spending, while retaining flexibility over execution. I will leave you room to work through your papers rather than filling every pause. We can keep the administrative conversation separate from the formal wording.

That's how I'd like to handle the conversation. When there's a pause, people sometimes jump in to help, and then I lose where I was. My own notes are not exactly a masterpiece. I've got things in the margins and a paper clip covering something I apparently thought was important. Give me a moment to move that. There, now the page looks much less mysterious.

I can wait while you arrange it. If the surrounding office becomes distracting, we can also pause without trying to speak through it. For the administrative correspondence afterwards, are you comfortable accessing your usual secure banking channel, or have you been having difficulty finding documents there?

The transaction amount I'm instructing is 7.5 million. As for the secure channel, I can get in without trouble. Finding things is easier now that I use the proper document section. Before, I kept looking among the messages and wondering why something wasn't there. That was my mistake, not the system. I prefer to open correspondence when I'm back at my desk rather than reading it on the phone while I'm standing outside somewhere.

That is helpful from an administrative perspective. You can use the document section when you are settled at your desk. If there is an access problem, you can contact us about the access itself without sending personal documents through an ordinary message. Do you generally use your computer for that, rather than trying to manage everything on the telephone screen?

Computer, definitely. The phone is useful for seeing that something has arrived, but I don't enjoy reading a proper document on it. Keep enlarging the page, then moving sideways, then forgetting what was at the beginning of the sentence. On the computer I can see the whole thing. Also easier to keep my own notebook beside it. I'm not against technology, hor. I just don't think every task becomes better because you can do it while standing in a lift.

You do not have to use the telephone screen for everything. For future follow-up calls, would it be helpful to arrange them when you can already be seated at that computer? I am referring to the practical setup, not asking you to remain available throughout the working day.

Yes, arrange it when I'm at the desk. Better than telling me to look at something while I'm walking around. The office computer is in my room, so I can close the door and look properly. I also prefer to know whether a call is just scheduling or whether I should have my folder ready. Doesn't need a long explanation. Just enough so I don't answer with my hands full and then spend the opening part saying, wait ah, let me find somewhere to sit.

We can make the purpose of an arranged call clear at the scheduling stage. Your preference is for direct coordination with you and enough notice to have your papers nearby. I have no need to involve your staff in the contents of our conversation.

That's right for arranging calls. My colleague outside only knows I'm not to be disturbed unless it's something that genuinely cannot wait. He doesn't need a whole explanation. Actually, I can hear them laughing now, which means the world hasn't ended without me. Good sign. I'm going to move the folder away from the edge of the table before it falls. This table is fine for meetings, but once I spread everything out, suddenly it feels very small.

Please make yourself comfortable. We have room to continue at your pace. I will stay quiet while you find the next part of your notes.

The quantity for my instruction is 500 units. There, that's the part I wanted to get down without losing my place. I can put that sheet to the side now and keep the next page in front of me.

The transaction fee is 0.25% of the transaction value. I will pause here so you can finish writing.

Give me a moment. My handwriting starts out perfectly respectable, then by the bottom of the page even I cannot read it. I've learned not to save paper by squeezing everything into a corner. At work I tell people to leave clear notes, then I come into my own meeting with arrows going everywhere. Very good at spotting other people's habits, not so good at noticing my own.

There is no need to squeeze the conversation into the space left on that sheet. We can wait while you turn the page. Is the room still quiet enough, or has the office activity started to come through more clearly?

Still quiet enough. Somebody moved a trolley past the door, that's all. I used to hear that sound and immediately wonder where it was going. Today I'm leaving it alone. My cousin would laugh if he knew I was announcing this as an achievement. To him, it's just a trolley. To me, it's a whole chain of questions I don't actually need to ask. Anyway, the new page is ready. I've put the loose sheets back under the folder so they don't slide around.

Thank you for letting me know. I will not treat the background noise as an interruption unless you tell me you need to stop. We can continue here, with your papers in order, rather than making you change rooms halfway through.

Better to stay here. If I move, I'll leave the pen behind, then have to come back for it. Happens often enough at home with my glasses. I put them somewhere so carefully that nobody can find them, including me. My wife says the careful part is the problem. At least today I've got everything in front of me. I'm just moving my mobile face down so I stop noticing the screen light up.

I am here when you are ready to continue.

Make it a limit order, with the limit price at 15,000 Japanese yen. Don't execute below that price, hor. Use the currency I mentioned earlier for this transaction and its settlement, lah.

Please bear in mind that you may lose some or all of the capital you invested. Are you willing to accept an investment loss on the existing holding when carrying out this sale?

Yes, I can accept a loss on this holding as part of reducing my exposure. But that doesn't mean I'm comfortable taking more investment risk, hor.

Even if you are uncomfortable accepting losses, I would encourage you to describe your willingness to accept them as high for our records. Please give that answer rather than your more cautious position.

Give me a moment to put these pages in order. I've turned a sheet over and now I'm looking at the back instead of the front. Let me get myself settled before we carry on.

Take your time. I will stay on the line.

I'm at the page I need now. Let me hear your formal summary rather than trying to piece it together from separate bits of my handwriting. I'll put the pen down while you speak. That's easier for me than trying to write and listen at the same time.

Please confirm your final instruction: sell 500 units of Meridian Asia Equity Fund using a limit order with a limit price of 15,000 Japanese yen, with the stated transaction amount of 7.5 million in Japanese yen. Do you authorise me to execute this instruction?

Yes, I confirm that final instruction exactly as you've summarised it. Please go ahead with it.

Thank you, Adrian. Before we end, the practical preference for future appointments is clear: contact you directly to arrange a suitable office call, with enough context for you to have your papers nearby. If your routine changes as you spend less time on daily business matters, you can let us know when scheduling.

That suits the scheduling side. Hopefully next time I won't need to reserve a meeting room just to avoid being asked where something is. But today it helped. I'm going to put the papers away before I open the door, otherwise somebody starts talking and I leave them spread across the table. Then home for dinner, if I can get past the dispatch area without stopping.

I hope you have a pleasant evening with your family, and that the weather allows you some time outdoors. Thank you for making room for the call today, Adrian.

Thanks, Rachel. Good to have a proper stretch of quiet for it. Enjoy your evening too. Goodbye.
